analysis.one_liner: Makes employers keep records on contractors, give written classification notices, and pay new penalties for misclassifying employees.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote; it died in committee when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend federal wage law to fight the practice of labeling workers as independent contractors when they are, in fact, employees. Employers would have to keep records on every contractor they engage, give written notice telling each worker how they were classified and where to complain, and face new civil penalties of up to $5,000 per misclassified worker, plus double wage damages when misclassification causes unpaid overtime or below-minimum pay. It would also require states, as a condition of federal unemployment grants, to audit employers who pay unreported wages and to penalize misclassification, and it would let Labor Department investigators share findings with the IRS.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who are treated as independent contractors but function as employees. Misclassified workers are denied overtime, minimum wage, unemployment insurance, workers' compensation, and employer payroll taxes, and they can be fired for complaining. The bill would create a written record of their classification, a presumption that a worker without proper records or notice is an employee, anti-retaliation protection that explicitly covers classification disputes, and doubled damages. State unemployment systems and the federal Treasury would also gain, because misclassification shifts payroll tax and unemployment insurance contributions away from employers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Misclassified workers and state unemployment funds

how_it_helps.text: Requires every employer to keep records on each contractor it engages and to give each new employee and contractor written notice of their classification, with instructions on how to contact the Labor Department if they suspect they have been misclassified.

Creates a legal presumption that a worker is an employee if the employer kept no records or gave no notice, and the employer can rebut it only with clear and convincing evidence — shifting the burden of proof to the employer.

Makes it unlawful to misclassify an employee and to fire or discriminate against anyone who complains about their classification, and doubles liquidated damages for minimum wage and overtime violations when the employer also misclassified the worker.

Adds civil penalties of up to $1,100 per violation, or up to $5,000 for repeat or willful violators, and requires the Wage and Hour Division to target audits at industries with frequent misclassification.

Conditions federal grants for state unemployment administration on states auditing employers who pay unreported wages and establishing their own penalties for misclassification, which restores unemployment insurance contributions lost to misclassification.

analysis.who_pays: Employers whose business model depends on classifying workers as independent contractors — in industries like trucking, construction, janitorial work, delivery, and staffing — would bear recordkeeping and notice costs, new penalties, exposure to double wage damages, and payroll-tax and unemployment-insurance back payments for workers reclassified as employees. State unemployment agencies would face new audit and enforcement duties as a condition of federal grants.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers using contractor and subcontracting labor

drawbacks.text: The recordkeeping, notice, and audit requirements would raise compliance costs for every business that legitimately engages independent contractors, not only those that misclassify, and small firms relying on contractor labor would feel the paperwork burden most.

The bill's presumption that a worker without proper records or notice is an employee — rebuttable only by clear and convincing evidence — would make independent contracting substantially riskier and could push some firms to stop using contractors or hire fewer people.

States would have to rewrite their unemployment laws to add audits and administrative penalties or risk conditions on federal grants, and the bill allows a delay for state legislative sessions, so its unemployment provisions would not take effect quickly.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers who are genuinely misclassified, the bill's notice, presumption, and doubled damages would have been a real enforcement tool at little cost to them. The costs fall on employers, and the strongest objection is that the recordkeeping and presumption rules would also burden businesses that classify workers correctly. On balance the bill is an enforcement measure aimed squarely at a known compliance gap, and its modest penalty caps ($1,100 per violation, $5,000 for willful violations) suggest a targeted design rather than a broad sweep.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in April 2010 and referred to the House Education and Labor Committee and the Ways and Means Committee; a month later it was sent to an Income Security and Family Support subcommittee, and neither committee ever reported it out before the Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Representative Lynn Woolsey introduced the bill on April 22, 2010, with Representatives Robert Andrews and George Miller as original cosponsors, and it was referred to the Education and Labor Committee and the Ways and Means Committee.
The bill had 19 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican cosponsors.
On May 3, 2010, it was referred to the Income Security and Family Support subcommittee, and the action history records no hearings, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action after that date.
The 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, without the bill receiving a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers whose business models rely on classifying workers as independent contractors are better off, because the recordkeeping, notice, presumption, and penalty provisions never took effect and misclassification remained cheaper than employment for many firms. Workers denied overtime and unemployment coverage by misclassification gained nothing.

industries.industry: Businesses relying on independent contractor labor (trucking, construction, janitorial, delivery, staffing)
industries.note: These firms would face recordkeeping and notice duties, penalties of up to $5,000 per misclassified worker, doubled wage damages, and payroll-tax and unemployment-insurance exposure for reclassified workers. Their savings from treating workers as contractors come directly out of those workers' overtime, unemployment, and payroll-tax protections.

The bill's records requirement covers workers engaged through entities such as companies or partnerships set up as a condition of the work, a structure common in subcontracting chains, so middlemen in these chains would face the same recordkeeping and presumption rules as direct employers.

States would have to audit employers who pay unreported wages and penalize misclassification as a condition of federal grants, restoring unemployment contributions and coverage that misclassification strips away.

industries.industry: U.S. Treasury and IRS payroll-tax collection
industries.note: The Labor Department's Wage and Hour Division could share misclassification findings with the IRS, and reclassifying workers as employees restores withheld payroll taxes.
